cards.q: Define a 'treaty' under general international law and under Art 2(1)(a) VCLT. Does the name of the document matter? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: A treaty is an agreement between subjects of international law governed by international law; the VCLT narrows this to written agreements between States — the name of the instrument is irrelevant, the intention to be legally bound decides.
• General (customary) definition: (1) an agreement, i.e. concordant expressions of will intended to create legal rights and obligations; (2) between two or more States or other subjects of international law (IOs, Holy See, ICRC); (3) governed by international law, not by the domestic law of one party.
• VCLT, Art 2(1)(a): an international agreement concluded between States in written form and governed by international law, whether embodied in a single instrument or in two or more related instruments (e.g. an exchange of notes) and whatever its particular designation.
• Designation irrelevant: treaty, convention, agreement, protocol, charter, covenant, pact, exchange of notes, even a 'declaration' or signed minutes. Cameroon v Nigeria (2002): the Maroua Declaration of two Heads of State was binding; Qatar v Bahrain (1994): signed minutes were an international agreement.
• Not treaties: political commitments/MoUs without intention to be bound (e.g. Helsinki Final Act 1975), contracts between States governed by domestic law (e.g. buying an embassy building), contracts between a State and a private company.
Memorise: Treaty = agreement + subjects of IL + governed by IL · VCLT adds States + written (Art 2(1)(a)) · name irrelevant, intention decides.

cards.q: In 1955 a sharp increase in lead levels was detected in the groundwater of the Xympora Peninsula. In 1956 the States Astamor and Balala concluded the 'Investigation Convention' to investigate and combat its cause. In 1982 Astamor, Balala and Cumo established the Xympora Regional Health Organisation (XRHO), an international organisation based in Balala, by the 'Xympora Health Charter'. In 1984 Cumo ratified an agreement with the XRHO, the 'Lead Crisis Understanding', to support Cumo in managing a local health crisis. In 1995 Astamor, Balala and Cumo concluded the 'LeadFree Pact' with the company HydroClean, commissioning it to build twenty purification plants. In 1996 the three States concluded the 'Debt Allocation Agreement', allocating among themselves the debts arising from the LeadFree project. To which of the agreements mentioned is the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties applicable, and why or why not? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The VCLT applies to the 1982 Xympora Health Charter and the 1996 Debt Allocation Agreement (provided the three States were VCLT parties when concluding them); it does not apply to the 1956 Investigation Convention, the 1984 Lead Crisis Understanding or the 1995 LeadFree Pact.
Test: the VCLT applies to agreements (a) between States (Art 1), (b) in written form and governed by international law, whatever their name (Art 2(1)(a)), (c) concluded after the VCLT entered into force for the States concerned (Art 4) — it has been in force since 27 January 1980. If the States were not VCLT parties, only custom applies.
• 1956 Investigation Convention (Astamor–Balala): an inter-State treaty, but concluded before 1980 → non-retroactivity (Art 4): VCLT not applicable as such; the customary rules it codifies apply.
• 1982 Xympora Health Charter: inter-State treaty concluded after 1980; as the constituent instrument of the XRHO it is expressly covered by Art 5 → VCLT applies, without prejudice to the relevant rules of the organization.
• 1984 Lead Crisis Understanding (Cumo–XRHO): a treaty (the name is irrelevant; 'ratified' shows the intention to be bound), but not between States → outside the VCLT (Art 1, 3); the 1986 Vienna Convention (States–IOs) is not in force → customary law.
• 1995 LeadFree Pact: HydroClean is a company, not a subject of international law; commissioning plants is a (domestic-law) contract → no treaty at all (ICJ Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. 1952).
• 1996 Debt Allocation Agreement: inter-State, concluded after 1980, allocating the debts among the States under international law → VCLT applies.
Memorise: VCLT = States + written + governed by IL + concluded after 27.1.1980 for them (Art 1, 2(1)(a), 4) · IO charters included (Art 5) · agreement with an IO → custom (Art 3) · company → no treaty.

cards.q: Variant (not an exam question): State Norvia (party to the VCLT since 1982) is involved in five agreements: (1) a written treaty on river navigation concluded with Sudalia (VCLT party since 1981) in 2012; (2) a written fisheries agreement concluded with Sudalia in 1974; (3) a written headquarters agreement concluded in 2018 with an international organization; (4) an agreement on a joint border commission reached orally by the two foreign ministers at a summit in 2021, never put in writing; (5) a 2020 concession contract with the multinational mining company TerraMin plc, governed by Norvian law. To which of these agreements is the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties applicable, and why or why not? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The VCLT applies only to agreement (1); (2)–(4) are treaties governed by customary law instead, and (5) is not a treaty at all.
Test: the VCLT applies as a convention to agreements (a) between States (Art 1), (b) in written form and governed by international law (Art 2(1)(a)), (c) concluded after the VCLT entered into force for the States concerned (Art 4).
• (1) 2012 navigation treaty: written, inter-State, both States bound by the VCLT before 2012 → VCLT applies.
• (2) 1974 fisheries agreement: concluded before the VCLT entered into force (27 Jan 1980) → non-retroactivity, Art 4; the same rules apply only insofar as they reflect custom.
• (3) Headquarters agreement with an IO: not between States → outside the VCLT (Art 1, 3). Still a treaty; the 1986 Vienna Convention (States–IOs) is not in force → customary law.
• (4) Oral agreement: not in written form → outside the VCLT, but Art 3(a): its legal force is unaffected; binding under custom if intended (cf. PCIJ Eastern Greenland 1933, Ihlen Declaration).
• (5) Concession contract: a company is no subject of international law and the contract is governed by domestic law → no treaty at all (ICJ Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. 1952) — neither the VCLT nor the customary law of treaties applies.
Memorise: VCLT = States + written + governed by IL + concluded after EIF for both (Art 1, 2(1)(a), 4) · oral agreement valid under custom (Art 3(a)) · company contracts ≠ treaties.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'Because France is not a party to the VCLT, the VCLT rules on reservations, interpretation and termination do not apply to a treaty concluded between France and Austria in 2015.' Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only partly — the VCLT does not apply as a treaty, but most of its rules bind France and Austria anyway as customary international law.
• A treaty binds only its parties (Art 34); France never became party, so the VCLT as a convention does not govern the treaty (Art 4 requires the VCLT to be in force for both States).
• But Art 3(b) and Art 4 reserve the rules that apply 'independently of the Convention', i.e. custom (see also Art 38). Most VCLT rules codify custom: the ICJ has treated Art 31–32 (interpretation; Libya/Chad 1994), Art 60 (Namibia 1971), Art 62 (Fisheries Jurisdiction 1973) and Art 60–62 generally (Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997) as customary law.
• Less clearly customary are procedural details such as Art 65–66 (conciliation, ICJ jurisdiction).
Memorise: Non-party → VCLT rules as custom (Art 3(b), 4, 38) · procedural Art 65–66 not clearly custom.

cards.q: When was the VCLT adopted and when did it enter into force? Explain the mechanism of its entry into force and from when Austria has been bound by it. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Adopted and opened for signature in Vienna in May 1969 (23 May 1969), in force since 27 January 1980; Austria acceded on 30 April 1979 but was bound only from 27 January 1980.
• '1969' is the date of adoption, not of entry into force.
• Art 84 VCLT: entry into force on the 30th day after deposit of the 35th instrument of ratification or accession; for every later State on the 30th day after its own deposit. The 35th instrument came in late December 1979 → objective EIF 27 Jan 1980.
• Austria deposited its instrument (30 Apr 1979) before the threshold was reached → it had to wait: subjective EIF for Austria = objective EIF, 27 Jan 1980. Switzerland, joining in 1990, was bound 30 days after its deposit.
• About 116 parties (2023) — far fewer than 193 UN members; for the rest the rules apply as custom. The 1986 Convention (States–IOs, IO–IO) is not yet in force.
Memorise: 1969 adopted · 27.1.1980 in force · Art 84 = 35 instruments + 30 days · Austria 30.4.1979 → bound 27.1.1980.

cards.q: The neighbouring States Aldoam, Bertus, Cilco and Daroto, together with the International Dairy Organization (IDAO), intend to conclude a treaty to reduce the environmental impact of rare earth mining — the Rare Earth Materials Treaty (REMT). The President of Aldoam, who leads the initiative, invites the Prime Ministers of Bertus and Daroto, the Environmental Minister of Cilco and the Secretary-General of the IDAO to an international conference to adopt the negotiated text and sign the treaty. Can these parties, represented by the invited officials, conclude such a treaty? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The four States can conclude REMT — the President and the two Prime Ministers act ex officio, Cilco's Environmental Minister needs full powers (or later confirmation) — but the IDAO most likely lacks the capacity to become party to a mining treaty (principle of speciality).
• Capacity: every State can conclude treaties (Art 6 VCLT); an IO only within its functions — its own rules (Art 6 VCLT 1986), principle of speciality (WHO Nuclear Weapons AO 1996), implied powers (Reparation 1949). Rare earth mining lies outside a dairy organization's tasks → IDAO would act ultra vires unless its founding treaty says otherwise.
• Representation: the President of Aldoam (Head of State) and the Prime Ministers of Bertus and Daroto (Heads of Government) may adopt and sign without full powers (Art 7(2)(a)). Cilco's Environmental Minister needs full powers (Art 7(1)(a)) or supporting practice (Art 7(1)(b)); otherwise no legal effect unless Cilco confirms (Art 8). IDAO's Secretary-General: no ex officio presumption — full powers or practice (Art 7(3)–(4) VCLT 1986).
• The VCLT 1969 governs only the relations among the four States (Art 3(c)); relations with the IDAO follow custom (1986 Convention not in force).
Memorise: Capacity: States Art 6 · IO = speciality (dairy ≠ mining) · Head of State/PM ex officio (7(2)(a)) · minister → full powers (7(1)) or Art 8 · IO head → full powers/practice (1986 Art 7(3)–(4)) · VCLT only among the States (Art 3(c)).

cards.q: Variant (not an exam question): The Global Milk Union (GMU), whose founding treaty entrusts it with 'promoting the production of and trade in milk products', signs a treaty with State Kalvia on the joint exploitation of lithium mines in Kalvia. Kalvia later insists that the GMU is bound; several GMU member States argue that the GMU had no power to conclude it. Who has capacity to conclude treaties, and is the GMU bound? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: States have full treaty-making capacity; an IO has it only within its functions (principle of speciality) — a mining treaty lies outside a dairy organization's competence, so it is ultra vires and does not validly bind the GMU.
• States: Art 6 VCLT — every State possesses capacity to conclude treaties (original, full legal personality).
• IOs: personality is derivative and functional — only the powers conferred in the founding treaty plus those necessarily implied for fulfilling its tasks (implied powers, Reparation for Injuries 1949). Art 6 of the 1986 Vienna Convention: an IO's capacity is governed by the rules of that organization. ICJ, WHO Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion (1996): IOs are governed by the principle of speciality.
• Application: lithium mining has no link to promoting milk products and is not necessary for the GMU's tasks → neither express nor implied power → ultra vires.
• Consequence: the GMU's consent is invalid; the violation is manifest (founding treaties are public and the mismatch is obvious to any partner acting in good faith — cf. Art 46(2) of the 1986 Convention), so the GMU may invoke it. Member States are not bound either (separate legal person).
Memorise: States = Art 6 full capacity · IOs = speciality + implied powers (WHO 1996, Reparation 1949) · outside competence = ultra vires, invalid.

cards.q: Variant (not an exam question): Esmar, Fontia and Gorvan conclude the Mining Standards Treaty, which according to its final clause becomes binding upon signature. At a conference in Fontia it is signed: for Esmar by its Minister of Mining, who has no full powers; for Fontia by its Prime Minister; for Gorvan by its ambassador accredited to Fontia. Earlier, the head of Gorvan's delegation to the conference had voted for the adoption of the text. Were these persons competent to act for their States, and what is the consequence of an act performed without authority? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only Fontia's Prime Minister bound his State ex officio; Esmar's Minister of Mining and Gorvan's ambassador needed full powers, so their signatures are without legal effect unless later confirmed (Art 8).
• Rule: a person represents a State if (a) he produces appropriate full powers (Art 7(1)(a), Art 2(1)(c)), or (b) the practice of the States concerned or other circumstances show that they intended to treat him as representative without full powers (Art 7(1)(b)).
• Ex officio (Art 7(2)): (a) Heads of State, Heads of Government, Foreign Ministers — all acts relating to conclusion (Cameroon v Nigeria 2002); (b) heads of diplomatic missions — only adopting the text of a treaty with the receiving State; (c) representatives to a conference/IO — only adopting the text in that forum.
• Fontia: Prime Minister = Head of Government → valid consent. Esmar: a sectoral minister is not listed; without full powers only Art 7(1)(b) could help → no authority. Gorvan: the ambassador may only adopt the text of a bilateral treaty with Fontia; this treaty is multilateral and signature here expresses consent → no authority. The delegation head's vote on adoption was valid (Art 7(2)(c), Art 9) but does not bind Gorvan.
• Art 8: an act performed by an unauthorized person is without legal effect unless afterwards confirmed by the State — expressly (subsequent full powers, ratification) or tacitly (performance, invoking the treaty).
Memorise: Big three = all acts (7(2)(a)) · ambassador / conference delegate = text only (7(2)(b)(c)) · others need full powers (7(1)) · unauthorized = no effect unless confirmed (Art 8).

cards.q: The head of the water department of Veltria's Ministry of Agriculture signed, without full powers, a bilateral agreement with Ostara on joint river monitoring, which binds upon signature. For three years Veltria published the agreement in its official gazette, submitted reports under it and received Ostara's monitoring data. A new government now claims Veltria was never bound because the official lacked authority. Is it right? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — the signature was initially without legal effect, but Veltria has confirmed it by its conduct (Art 8 VCLT), so it is bound.
• The official is not an ex officio representative (Art 7(2)) and had no full powers (Art 7(1)(a)) → under Art 8 his act had no legal effect unless afterwards confirmed by Veltria.
• Confirmation needs no particular form: it may be express or implied from conduct showing that the State treats the treaty as binding. Publication in the official gazette, performance and acceptance of benefits over three years amount to tacit confirmation.
• Good faith (estoppel, cf. the acquiescence idea of Art 45(b)) bars Veltria from now relying on the defect. It can only leave through the treaty's clause or the termination grounds (Art 54 ff.).
Memorise: No authority → Art 8 no effect · confirmation express or by conduct → bound · later objection = venire contra factum proprium.

cards.q: The Foreign Minister of Castora signed a boundary treaty with Pellia which, by its terms, binds upon signature. Castora's published constitution requires parliamentary approval of all boundary treaties; parliament was never consulted. Five years later, after performing the treaty, Castora claims that it is invalid. Assess. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Castora is almost certainly bound: an internal rule on competence can be invoked only if its violation was manifest and concerned a rule of fundamental importance (Art 46), and a Foreign Minister's authority is presumed.
• Art 27: internal law is no justification for non-performance — without prejudice to Art 46.
• Art 46(1): consent expressed in violation of internal law regarding competence to conclude treaties invalidates consent only if the violation was (a) manifest and (b) concerned a rule of internal law of fundamental importance. Art 46(2): manifest = objectively evident to any State conducting itself in accordance with normal practice and in good faith.
• Application: parliamentary approval is a rule of fundamental importance. But the Foreign Minister is one of the 'big three' presumed to represent the State for all acts (Art 7(2)(a)); Pellia could rely on that. Cameroon v Nigeria (2002): no general duty to follow other States' constitutional law; a limitation on such an organ is not manifest unless at least properly publicized — there, Nigeria's constitutional requirement did not make the violation manifest.
• In addition, five years of performance = acquiescence → right lost (Art 45(b)).
Memorise: Art 27 + Art 46: manifest + fundamental importance · big three presumed · Cameroon v Nigeria · Art 45 loss of right.

cards.q: In 2023 the Foreign Minister of State Antica signed the UNESCO 'Convention for the Protection of Ancient Monuments', which is subject to ratification and obliges parties to protect certain buildings against demolition and major alterations. What further steps are required, internationally and domestically, for the Convention to bind and be applied in Antica? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Signature subject to ratification does not yet bind; Antica must obtain domestic approval, ratify, deposit its instrument, the Convention must enter into force (for Antica), and it must be registered and published.
• Domestic approval under Antica's constitution (e.g. parliamentary approval) — the internal half of ratification.
• Ratification (Art 14, Art 2(1)(b) VCLT): the international act establishing consent to be bound, issued by a competent organ (usually the Head of State, Art 7(2)(a)).
• Deposit of the instrument with the depositary (UNESCO Director-General); consent is established upon deposit (Art 16(b)); bilateral treaties: exchange.
• Entry into force (Art 24): objectively when the Convention's conditions are met (number of ratifications + waiting period); for Antica on its own date if it ratifies later (Art 24(3)). Only then is Antica a party bound under Art 26.
• Registration with the UN Secretariat and publication (Art 102 UN Charter, Art 80 VCLT); domestic publication in the official gazette and, where needed, implementing legislation so that authorities and courts can apply it.
• Meanwhile Art 18: as a signatory Antica must not defeat the object and purpose (e.g. not demolish the temples) until it declares it will not ratify.
Memorise: Sign → domestic approval → ratify → deposit → EIF (objective/subjective) → register (Art 102) → publish · Art 18 in between.

cards.q: After a change of government in Antica, the new head of government (i) claims that the Foreign Minister who signed the UNESCO Monuments Convention was not competent under international law to sign on behalf of the State, and (ii) declares the Convention void because it violates Antica's domestic building law. How will Antica's International Law Office respond? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both arguments fail — a Foreign Minister represents the State ex officio, and domestic law can neither invalidate a treaty nor justify its non-performance.
• (i) Consent to be bound can be expressed by persons with full powers (Art 7(1)) and, without full powers, by the Head of State, Head of Government and Foreign Minister for all acts (Art 7(2)(a)). The signature was valid. If the Convention requires ratification, the signature did not yet bind: the government may simply not ratify and declare so (ending the Art 18 duty).
• (ii) Art 27: a party may not invoke its internal law as justification for failure to perform. A conflict with ordinary legislation is no ground of invalidity — validity can be impeached only under the VCLT (Art 42). Only Art 46 (manifest violation of a fundamental internal rule on competence to conclude treaties) could help — a building law is no competence rule.
• If Antica is already bound, it must adapt its law or leave lawfully (withdrawal clause, Art 54 ff.); otherwise it incurs state responsibility.
Memorise: FM = big three (7(2)(a)) · Art 27 internal law no excuse · Art 42 exhaustive grounds · only Art 46 (competence, manifest).

cards.q: Distinguish the adoption, the authentication and the expression of consent to be bound of a treaty. Which rules of the VCLT apply to each step? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Adoption fixes the content of the text, authentication certifies it as authentic and definitive, and consent to be bound is the act by which a State becomes bound — three separate steps.
• Adoption (Art 9): by consent of all States participating in drawing it up; at an international conference by two thirds of the States present and voting, unless they decide by the same majority to apply a different rule.
• Authentication (Art 10): the text is established as authentic and definitive by the procedure provided in it or agreed, failing which by signature, signature ad referendum or initialling of the text or of the Final Act of the conference. Afterwards changes only by agreement (errors: Art 79).
• Consent to be bound (Art 11–17): signature, exchange of instruments, ratification, acceptance, approval, accession or any other agreed means; established by exchange, deposit or notification (Art 16).
• Throughout, representatives need full powers or ex officio authority (Art 7); the final clauses apply from adoption (Art 24(4)).
Memorise: Adopt (Art 9: all / 2/3 present and voting) → authenticate (Art 10: sign, ad referendum, initial) → consent (Art 11–16) · Art 24(4) from adoption.

cards.q: At a diplomatic conference attended by 120 States the text of a convention is put to the vote: 70 States vote in favour, 30 against and 20 abstain. The rules of procedure say nothing on majorities. Has the text been adopted? Would the result differ with 65 in favour, 35 against and 20 abstentions? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes in the first scenario (70 of 100 votes cast = 70 % ≥ 2/3), no in the second (65 of 100 = 65 % < 2/3).
• Art 9(2) VCLT: at an international conference a text is adopted by two thirds of the States present and voting, unless they decide by the same majority to apply a different rule.
• 'Present and voting' = States casting a yes or no vote; abstentions are not counted (UN practice).
• Scenario 1: 70 + 30 = 100 voting → 2/3 = 66.7 → 67 needed → 70 → adopted. Scenario 2: 65 + 35 = 100 → 65 < 67 → not adopted, although a clear majority.
• Outside a conference, adoption requires the consent of all participating States (Art 9(1)). Adoption binds nobody — it only fixes the text.
Memorise: Art 9(2) = 2/3 of present AND voting · abstentions out · adoption ≠ consent to be bound.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'As soon as a State's representative has signed a treaty, the State is bound by it.' Distinguish the simplified procedure from the procedure requiring ratification. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — signature binds only in the simplified procedure; where ratification is required, signature merely authenticates the text, makes the State a signatory and triggers the Art 18 duty.
• Simplified procedure: negotiation → (optional initialling) → signature or exchange of instruments. Signature expresses consent where the treaty so provides, the negotiating States so agreed, or this intention appears from the full powers or the negotiations (Art 12(1)); initialling counts as signature if so agreed, signature ad referendum becomes full signature when confirmed (Art 12(2)). Example: the 2006 Austria–Hungary agreement on missions abroad, in force on signature.
• Ratification procedure: negotiation → signature → domestic approval → ratification (Art 14: required if the treaty so provides, it was agreed, the representative signed 'subject to ratification', or this intention appears). The State is bound only from ratification and entry into force.
• A mere signature: authentication (Art 10), right to ratify, obligation not to defeat the object and purpose (Art 18) — but no duty to ratify.
Memorise: Simplified: signature = consent (Art 12) · long route: sign → approve → ratify (Art 14) · signature alone = Art 18 only.

cards.q: Distinguish ratification, accession and acceptance/approval. When is a State's consent established, and who is a depositary? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All are international acts by which a State establishes its consent to be bound (Art 2(1)(b)) with identical effect; they differ only in what precedes them — and consent is established on exchange, deposit or notification (Art 16).
• Ratification (Art 14): confirms a prior signature made subject to ratification; rests on domestic approval.
• Accession (Art 15): a single act by a State that did not sign — e.g. after the signature period closed; possible if the treaty provides for it or the parties agree. Austria acceded to the VCLT in 1979.
• Acceptance/approval (Art 14(2)): function like ratification, often with a lighter internal procedure.
• Art 16: consent is established by exchange between the contracting States (bilateral), deposit with the depositary (multilateral), or notification if agreed. The depositary (Art 76–77) — a State, an IO or its chief officer (often the UN Secretary-General) — keeps the originals, receives instruments and informs the States (e.g. when the EIF threshold is reached).
Memorise: Ratify = after signature · accede = without signature · accept/approve = ratification-light · same effect (Art 2(1)(b)) · Art 16 exchange/deposit/notification.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'A treaty that has not been registered with the UN Secretariat is invalid.' Explain the registration requirement and its purpose. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — non-registration does not affect validity; it only prevents the parties from invoking the treaty before any organ of the United Nations.
• Art 102(1) UN Charter: every treaty and international agreement entered into by a UN Member after 1945 shall as soon as possible be registered with and published by the Secretariat (UN Treaty Series). Art 80 VCLT: after entry into force treaties are transmitted to the Secretariat for registration (or filing and recording) and publication.
• Sanction, Art 102(2): an unregistered treaty cannot be invoked before any UN organ, including the ICJ. Between the parties it remains valid and binding — ICJ, Qatar v Bahrain (1994): non-registration or late registration does not affect the validity of the agreement.
• Purpose: to end secret diplomacy and make treaty relations transparent (Wilson's 'open covenants'; Art 18 League Covenant, which went further and denied binding force to unregistered treaties).
Memorise: Art 102 Charter + Art 80 VCLT · sanction = not invocable before UN organs (ICJ) · still valid (Qatar v Bahrain 1994) · purpose: no secret treaties.

cards.q: Explain the rules on the entry into force of a treaty under the VCLT, the difference between objective and subjective entry into force, and which treaty provisions apply before entry into force. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: A treaty enters into force as it provides or as the negotiating States agree, failing which when all negotiating States have consented; a later joiner is bound from its own date; final clauses, provisional application and Art 18 operate earlier.
• Art 24(1): in the manner and on the date the treaty provides or the negotiating States agree — typically a number of instruments plus a waiting period (Art 84 VCLT: 35 instruments + 30 days; Paris Agreement: 55 parties with 55 % of emissions + 30 days).
• Art 24(2): failing such provision, as soon as consent to be bound has been established for all negotiating States — a single refusal blocks it.
• Art 24(3): consent established after entry into force → the treaty enters into force for that State on that date, unless the treaty provides otherwise (usually its own waiting period).
• Objective EIF = the treaty exists as binding law at all; subjective EIF = date it binds a particular State. Early ratifiers wait for the objective date; late joiners get their own date — always answer both.
• Before EIF: Art 24(4) — clauses on authentication, consent, manner and date of EIF, reservations, depositary and other matters necessarily arising before EIF apply from adoption of the text; Art 25 provisional application if provided or agreed; Art 18 interim duty.
Memorise: 24(1) as agreed · 24(2) all negotiating States · 24(3) later = own date · objective vs subjective · 24(4) final clauses from adoption · Art 25 provisional.

cards.q: Five neighbouring States A–E negotiate a treaty against deforestation. Art XI reads: '1. The present Treaty shall be ratified. 2. The present Treaty shall enter into force six months after the deposit of three instruments of ratification. As regards any High Contracting Party ratifying subsequently, the Treaty shall come into force 30 days after the deposit of its instrument of ratification.' The text was adopted on 15.09.2014; A, B and E signed on 03.10.2014, C and D on 10.10.2014. Ratifications (each deposited the same day): B 31.10.2014, C 07.01.2015, A 15.02.2015, D 24.08.2015, E 13.06.2016. When did the treaty enter into force? When did it enter into force for A, D and E? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Objective entry into force on 15.08.2015 — also for A (and B, C); for D on 23.09.2015; for E on 13.07.2016.
• Order of deposits: B (1st, 31.10.2014), C (2nd, 07.01.2015), A (3rd, 15.02.2015). Six months after the third deposit → 15.08.2015 = objective EIF (Art 24(1)).
• A, B and C ratified before that date → bound from 15.08.2015 (subjective = objective EIF).
• D deposited on 24.08.2015, i.e. after EIF → second sentence: 30 days after deposit → 23.09.2015 (7 remaining days of August + 23 days of September; Art 24(3)).
• E deposited on 13.06.2016 → 30 days → 13.07.2016 (17 days of June + 13 of July).
• Signature dates are irrelevant for EIF (ratification required); they matter only for Art 18.
Memorise: Find the 3rd deposit + 6 months = objective EIF · early ratifiers wait · later ones: own deposit + 30 days.

cards.q: A deforestation treaty requires ratification; its text was adopted on 15.09.2014. States A and B signed on 03.10.2014; B ratified on 31.10.2014 and A on 15.02.2015; the treaty entered into force on 15.08.2015. What obligations are binding upon the contracting States before the treaty enters into force, and when do these obligations take effect for A and B? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Before entry into force only the interim obligation not to defeat the object and purpose (Art 18) and the final clauses (Art 24(4)) bind; for both A and B Art 18 applies from signature on 03.10.2014 until EIF on 15.08.2015.
• Art 18(a): a State that has signed subject to ratification must refrain from acts which would defeat the object and purpose until it has made clear its intention not to become a party. Art 18(b): the same after it has expressed consent to be bound, pending entry into force and provided EIF is not unduly delayed. Only a duty of abstention (e.g. no mass clear-cutting of the forests to be protected), not a duty to perform.
• Art 24(4): provisions on authentication, consent, manner and date of EIF, reservations, depositary functions and other matters necessarily arising before EIF (e.g. Art XI itself) apply from the adoption of the text — 15.09.2014, for all negotiating States.
• A: Art 18(a) from 03.10.2014; Art 18(b) from ratification on 15.02.2015; full obligations (Art 26) from 15.08.2015.
• B: Art 18(a) from 03.10.2014; Art 18(b) from 31.10.2014; bound from 15.08.2015. Some nine months' wait is not 'undue delay'.
Memorise: Before EIF: Art 18 (a) signatory / (b) ratifier + Art 24(4) final clauses from adoption · after EIF: Art 26.

cards.q: State A is party to a multilateral treaty against deforestation. Its territory includes a large archipelago in the Pacific Ocean covered by rainforest with rare tree species, which A now wants to fell. State E protests that the treaty forbids this. The treaty contains no provision on its territorial application. Is the treaty applicable to the archipelago? What could have been done to achieve the opposite result? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes — a treaty binds each party in respect of its entire territory (Art 29 VCLT); A would have needed a territorial exclusion clause or a permitted territorial declaration/reservation.
• Art 29: unless a different intention appears from the treaty or is otherwise established, a treaty is binding upon each party in respect of its entire territory — including distant islands and overseas parts. No different intention appears → the treaty covers the archipelago; felling would breach it (Art 26).
• Opposite result: (1) a territorial application clause in the treaty excluding the archipelago or allowing States to extend/exclude territories by declaration (cf. Art 56 ECHR; Danish declarations concerning the Faroe Islands); (2) a declaration or reservation excluding the archipelago upon signature or ratification, if not prohibited and accepted (Art 19–21) — though excluding the most valuable forest may clash with the object and purpose; (3) a different intention otherwise established, e.g. an agreement of all parties.
Memorise: Art 29: entire territory unless otherwise intended · exclude via territorial clause or declaration/reservation at the time of consent.

cards.q: A treaty is authentic in the five official languages of its contracting parties. How are such multilingual treaties interpreted? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All authentic texts are equally authoritative and presumed to have the same meaning; divergences are resolved first with Art 31–32 and then by the meaning that best reconciles the texts in the light of the object and purpose (Art 33).
• Art 33(1): the text is equally authoritative in each language, unless the treaty provides or the parties agree that a particular text prevails in case of divergence ('the English text shall prevail').
• Art 33(2): a version in a language other than the authenticated ones is authentic only if the treaty so provides or the parties so agree — official translations are not.
• Art 33(3): the terms are presumed to have the same meaning in each authentic text.
• Art 33(4): if a comparison discloses a difference of meaning which the application of Art 31 and 32 does not remove, the meaning which best reconciles the texts, having regard to the object and purpose, is adopted.
• Example: LaGrand (ICJ 2001) — English 'indicate … ought to be taken' vs French 'doivent être prises' in Art 41 ICJ Statute; applying Art 33(4) and the Statute's object and purpose, provisional measures are binding.
Memorise: Art 33: equal authority · same meaning presumed · Art 31–32 first · then best reconciliation by object and purpose · unless a prevailing-text clause.

cards.q: States A, B, C and D adopt a treaty on artificial intelligence which is open to accession. Art XV: it enters into force on the first day of the month following the date of deposit of the fourth instrument of ratification; for each State acceding thereafter, on the first day of the month that follows the fifteenth day after the deposit of its instrument of accession. All four sign on 2 February 2024. B deposits its instrument of ratification on 10 February, C on 20 March and D on 15 April 2024. After a change of government, A declares that it will not ratify. States E and F, which did not sign, deposit their instruments on 10 June 2024 (E) and 12 September 2024 (F). When does the treaty enter into force for each State? Distinguish objective and subjective entry into force. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Objective entry into force on 1 July 2024 (also for B, C, D and E); for F on 1 October 2024; for A never.
• After D's deposit (15 April) there are only three instruments — A's refusal blocks entry into force.
• E's instrument of 10 June 2024 is the fourth. Although E accedes rather than ratifies, accession has the same effect (Art 2(1)(b), 15) and the treaty is expressly open to accession; a good-faith reading (Art 31) counts it — otherwise the treaty could never enter into force without A. → Objective EIF: first day of the month following 10 June = 1 July 2024.
• B, C and D (early ratifiers): subjective EIF = 1 July 2024.
• E: 1 July 2024 — the same under the accession formula (10 June + 15 days = 25 June → 1 July).
• F: accedes after EIF → 12 September + 15 days = 27 September → first day of the following month = 1 October 2024 (Art 24(3)).
• A: signatory only, never a party → no entry into force for A.
Memorise: Find the 4th instrument (accessions count) → 1st of next month = objective EIF · later joiners: deposit + 15 days → 1st of next month.

cards.q: State A signed a treaty on artificial intelligence on 2 February 2024; the treaty requires ratification. After a change of government in February 2024, A's new digitalization minister calls the treaty a restriction of free competition, and A declares to the other States that it will not ratify. The treaty enters into force among the other States on 1 July 2024. Is State A bound by the treaty? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — A never expressed consent to be bound, and its only obligation (Art 18) ended when it declared that it would not ratify.
• A treaty subject to ratification binds a State only after ratification (Art 14) and entry into force (Art 24, 26). Signature made A a signatory — not a contracting State or party (Art 2(1)(f)–(g)); there is no duty to ratify.
• Art 18(a): as a signatory A had to refrain from acts that would defeat the object and purpose 'until it shall have made its intention clear not to become a party'. Its declaration to the other States ended this duty (cf. the US notification on the Rome Statute in 2002).
• For A the treaty is res inter alios acta (Art 34); A is bound only by customary rules the treaty may reflect (Art 38).
Memorise: Signature ≠ consent (Art 14) · Art 18 ends with a clear declaration · non-party = Art 34 (only custom, Art 38).

cards.q: The contracting States of a treaty on artificial intelligence disagree on the interpretation of its provisions on prohibited uses of AI. What are the methods of treaty interpretation in international law? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Art 31 VCLT lays down one general rule — good faith, ordinary meaning, context, object and purpose, plus subsequent agreements and practice — and Art 32 adds the travaux préparatoires as supplementary means.
• Good faith as the overarching principle (Art 31(1)).
• Textual: ordinary meaning of the terms (Art 31(1)); a special meaning only if the parties so intended (Art 31(4)).
• Systematic: context = text with preamble and annexes, agreements and instruments made in connection with the conclusion (Art 31(2)); together with subsequent agreements, subsequent practice establishing the parties' agreement and relevant rules of international law between the parties (Art 31(3)).
• Teleological: object and purpose, effet utile (for IOs implied powers).
• Historical (supplementary, Art 32): preparatory work and circumstances of conclusion.
• All Art 31 elements are of equal rank and applied together as a single operation — objective, text-oriented approach.
Memorise: Art 31 = good faith + text + context + object/purpose (+ subsequent practice), one operation · Art 32 travaux supplementary · Art 33 languages.

cards.q: In a dispute over the interpretation of a treaty on artificial intelligence, State C relies on the negotiation protocols. States E and F object because they acceded later and did not take part in the negotiations. Which method of interpretation does C refer to, under what circumstances would it be relevant, and what are the underlying problems? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: C invokes historical interpretation by means of the travaux préparatoires — a supplementary means (Art 32) that may confirm the Art 31 result or decide only if that result is ambiguous or absurd; its use against acceding States is problematic.
• Art 32: recourse to the preparatory work and the circumstances of conclusion (a) to confirm the meaning resulting from Art 31, or (b) to determine the meaning when Art 31 leaves it ambiguous or obscure or leads to a manifestly absurd or unreasonable result. (It is not teleological interpretation.)
• Problems: travaux are often incomplete or unpublished and reflect positions of individual delegations, not agreement; acceding States E and F could not shape them and relied on the text. PCIJ, River Oder Commission (1929): travaux were not used against States that had not participated in them. Today published travaux may be used, since acceding States could consult them — but with less weight.
Memorise: Travaux = historical, Art 32: confirm, or decide if ambiguous/absurd · acceding States not involved (River Oder 1929) → caution.

cards.q: When may recourse be had to the travaux préparatoires to assist in interpreting a treaty? Is it correct that they may only be consulted when the text is ambiguous? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Under Art 32 VCLT travaux may always be used to confirm the meaning reached under Art 31, but may determine the meaning only if Art 31 leaves it ambiguous or obscure or leads to a manifestly absurd or unreasonable result — so the statement is too narrow.
• Travaux préparatoires (drafts, negotiation records, conference minutes) and the circumstances of conclusion are supplementary means, subordinate to the general rule of Art 31.
• Confirmation: always permissible, even for a clear text (courts regularly 'confirm' their Art 31 reading with the drafting history).
• Determination: only if the Art 31 interpretation (a) leaves the meaning ambiguous or obscure, or (b) leads to a manifestly absurd or unreasonable result.
• Limits: travaux cannot override a clear text; caution towards States that acceded later and did not participate.
Memorise: Art 32: confirm = always · determine = only if ambiguous/obscure or absurd/unreasonable.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'Whenever one party to a treaty consistently applies a provision in a certain way, that practice becomes the authoritative interpretation of the treaty.' (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — only subsequent practice that establishes the agreement of the parties counts as authentic interpretation (Art 31(3)(b)); one party's practice is merely its own view.
• Interpretation is decentralized: each party interprets for itself unless the treaty creates an authoritative interpreter (e.g. ECtHR under Art 32 ECHR, the ICJ under a compromissory clause).
• Art 31(3): together with the context account is taken of (a) subsequent agreements between the parties on interpretation or application, (b) subsequent practice establishing the agreement of the parties — practice of all parties or accepted by them, (c) relevant rules of international law applicable between the parties.
• One party's consistent practice, if others protest, does not establish agreement; it may be evidence or found acquiescence/estoppel.
Memorise: Art 31(3)(b): practice establishing agreement of ALL parties · one party ≠ authentic interpretation · interpretation decentralized.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'A statement that a State calls an "interpretative declaration" can never be a reservation.' Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — whether a statement is a reservation depends on its content, not its label ('however phrased or named', Art 2(1)(d)).
• Reservation, Art 2(1)(d): a unilateral statement, however phrased or named, made when signing, ratifying, accepting, approving or acceding, whereby a State purports to exclude or to modify the legal effect of certain provisions of the treaty in their application to that State.
• Interpretative declaration: only clarifies the meaning a State attributes to a provision, without changing its legal effect; not subject to Art 19–23.
• Test: does the statement exclude or modify legal effect? Then it is a reservation and must satisfy Art 19–23. ECtHR, Belilos v Switzerland (1988): a Swiss 'interpretative declaration' on Art 6 ECHR was in substance a reservation — and invalid.
Memorise: Substance over label · exclude/modify = reservation (Art 2(1)(d)) · merely clarify = interpretative declaration · Belilos 1988.

cards.q: What are the requirements for a valid reservation to a multilateral treaty? Address timing, form and substantive admissibility. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: A reservation must be formulated at signature or when consent is expressed, in writing and communicated, and must not be excluded under Art 19 (prohibited, not among permitted ones, or incompatible with object and purpose).
• Qualification: a statement excluding or modifying the legal effect of certain provisions (Art 2(1)(d)).
• Timing (Art 19 chapeau): when signing, ratifying, accepting, approving or acceding. A reservation made on signature of a treaty subject to ratification must be formally confirmed on ratification and counts as made then (Art 23(2)). Later reservations only if no other contracting State objects (ILC Guide to Practice 2011).
• Form (Art 23(1)): in writing, communicated to the contracting States and other States entitled to become parties (via the depositary); the same for acceptances, objections and withdrawals (Art 23(4)).
• Substance (Art 19): not admissible if (a) the treaty prohibits reservations (e.g. Art 120 Rome Statute); (b) the treaty permits only specified reservations and this is not one; (c) otherwise, it is incompatible with the object and purpose (ICJ Genocide Convention AO 1951) — e.g. vague general reservations subordinating the whole treaty to domestic or religious law.
• Then acceptance: expressly authorized reservations need none (Art 20(1)); otherwise Art 20(2)–(5).
Memorise: Definition → timing (sign/ratify/accede; confirm at ratification) → writing + communicated (Art 23) → Art 19 (a)(b)(c) → acceptance (Art 20).

cards.q: Explain the legal effects of acceptance of and objection to a reservation under Art 20 and 21 VCLT. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Acceptance (express, or tacit after 12 months) creates treaty relations modified by the reservation; a simple objection keeps the treaty in force minus the reserved provision; a qualified objection excludes treaty relations between the two States.
• Background: since the Genocide Convention AO (1951) a flexible system replaced unanimity — the multilateral treaty splits into bilateral relations.
• Special cases: expressly authorized reservations need no acceptance (Art 20(1)); unanimous acceptance where a limited number of negotiating States makes integrity essential (Art 20(2)); constituent instruments of IOs need acceptance by the competent organ (Art 20(3)).
• Acceptance (Art 20(4)(a)): the reserving State becomes a party in relation to the accepting State. Tacit acceptance (Art 20(5)): no objection within 12 months after notification or by the date of own consent, whichever is later. Consent containing a reservation is effective once at least one contracting State has accepted it (Art 20(4)(c)).
• Effect (Art 21(1)): the provisions are modified to the extent of the reservation for the reserving State and reciprocally for the other party; relations among the other parties are untouched (Art 21(2)).
• Simple objection (Art 20(4)(b), 21(3)): treaty in force between the two, but the provisions to which the reservation relates do not apply between them to the extent of the reservation (e.g. Austria's objection to Saudi Arabia's CEDAW reservation).
• Qualified objection: the objecting State definitely expresses that the treaty shall not enter into force between them → no treaty relations (Art 20(4)(b)).
Memorise: Accept (express / 12 months' silence) → modified, reciprocal (21(1)) · simple objection → treaty minus provision (21(3)) · qualified → no relations (20(4)(b)).

cards.q: Alandia, Bergamont and Chiemera border Lake Barbara, used mainly for tourism and fishing and also of interest to scientists. On 24 May 2024 their Ministers of Tourism sign the 'Treaty on the Use of Lake Barbara for Tourism and Other Economic Purposes' at a special event; it enters into force on the 20th day after ratification by two signatory States. Alandia deposits its instrument of ratification with the depositary Bergamont on 15 June 2024. Bergamont ratifies on 23 October 2024 with a reservation excluding the research provisions. Alandia submits a written protest against the reservation on 21 November 2024; Chiemera no longer wants to ratify. Has the treaty entered into force? If yes, when? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes — on 12 November 2024.
• Rule: Art 24(1) VCLT — a treaty enters into force in the manner and on the date it provides; here on the 20th day after the second ratification.
• Application: 2nd ratification = Bergamont, 23 October 2024; 24–31 October = 8 days + 1–12 November = 12 days → 12 November 2024. Chiemera is not needed; Alandia's simple objection does not block entry into force (Art 20(4)(b)).
• Extra: a ratification with a reservation is effective once another contracting State accepts it (Art 20(4)(c)); depositary practice counts it on deposit anyway.
Memorise: 2nd ratification 23.10.2024 + 20 days = 12.11.2024 · a simple objection does not block entry into force.

cards.q: Alandia, Bergamont and Chiemera border Lake Barbara, used mainly for tourism and fishing and also of interest to scientists. On 24 May 2024 their Ministers of Tourism sign the 'Treaty on the Use of Lake Barbara for Tourism and Other Economic Purposes' at a special event; it enters into force on the 20th day after ratification by two signatory States. The treaty contains no provision on reservations. Upon ratification on 23 October 2024 Bergamont, to appease its opposition, declares in writing: 'Bergamont is not bound by those parts of the treaty that concern research activities in and around Lake Barbara.' Is the reservation admissible? Examine the conditions. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes, most likely — it is a genuine reservation, made at a permitted time and in writing, the treaty does not exclude it, and it does not defeat the treaty's object and purpose; open point: with only three negotiating States all parties may have to accept it (Art 20(2)).
• Check 1 — reservation? A unilateral statement made upon ratification excluding the legal effect of certain provisions for Bergamont → yes (Art 2(1)(d)).
• Check 2 — timing: formulated upon ratification → permitted (Art 19 chapeau: signature, ratification, acceptance, approval, accession).
• Check 3 — form: in writing and communicated to the contracting and signatory States (Art 23(1)); as depositary Bergamont must notify Alandia and Chiemera (Art 77(1)(e)).
• Check 4 — Art 19(a)–(b): the treaty neither prohibits reservations nor permits only specified ones.
• Check 5 — Art 19(c) object and purpose: the treaty concerns tourism and other economic uses of the lake; research is a side aspect → compatible. (Minor weakness: the articles are not named, but the excluded part is identifiable.)
• Check 6 — acceptance regime: if the limited number of negotiating States and the object and purpose show that applying the whole treaty is an essential condition of each State's consent, all parties must accept (Art 20(2)) — Alandia's objection would then block the reservation. As research is peripheral, the normal regime of Art 20(4)–(5) more likely applies.
• Result: admissible; its effect towards each State depends on that State's reaction (Art 20–21).
Memorise: Reservation? (2(1)(d)) → timing (19) → writing + notification (23) → 19(a)(b)(c) → small group: Art 20(2)? → effects 20(4)/21.

cards.q: Alandia, Bergamont and Chiemera border Lake Barbara, used mainly for tourism and fishing and also of interest to scientists. On 24 May 2024 their Ministers of Tourism sign the 'Treaty on the Use of Lake Barbara for Tourism and Other Economic Purposes' at a special event; it enters into force on the 20th day after ratification by two signatory States. Bergamont (the depositary) ratifies on 23 October 2024 with a reservation excluding the treaty's research provisions and notifies it the same day. Alandia, which ratified on 15 June 2024, submits a written protest against the reservation on 21 November 2024, without saying anything about the treaty's entry into force between itself and Bergamont. Is Alandia's protest timely? Why (not)? What is its legal effect? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes, it is timely — Alandia had 12 months from notification, i.e. until about 23 October 2025 (Art 20(5)); as a simple objection it keeps the treaty in force between Alandia and Bergamont, but without the research provisions (Art 21(3)).
• Nature and form: a written protest against a reservation is an objection; it must be in writing and communicated (Art 23(1)) → satisfied.
• Timeliness — rule (Art 20(5)): a State is deemed to have accepted a reservation if it has not objected by the end of 12 months after notification or by the date of its own consent to be bound, whichever is later. Application: Alandia consented earlier, so 12 months from notification (23 October 2024) apply → 21 November 2024 is in time (entry into force is not the criterion).
• Effect — rule: an objection does not preclude entry into force between the objecting and the reserving State unless the objecting State definitely expresses that intention (Art 20(4)(b)); the provisions to which the reservation relates then do not apply between them to the extent of the reservation (Art 21(3)). Application: simple objection → treaty applies between Alandia and Bergamont without the research provisions (for an excluding reservation practically like acceptance).
• Alternatives: a qualified objection would exclude all treaty relations between the two — with Chiemera out, the treaty would then apply between no one; if Art 20(2) applied, the objection would prevent the reservation from being established.
Memorise: Deadline = later of notification + 12 months and own consent (20(5)) · simple objection → treaty minus provision (21(3)) · qualified → no relations (20(4)(b)).

cards.q: Alandia, Bergamont and Chiemera border Lake Barbara, used mainly for tourism and fishing and also of interest to scientists. On 24 May 2024 their Ministers of Tourism sign the 'Treaty on the Use of Lake Barbara for Tourism and Other Economic Purposes' at a special event; it enters into force on the 20th day after ratification by two signatory States. Chiemera signed through its Minister of Tourism but, after Bergamont's reservation, is no longer willing to ratify; the treaty has entered into force between Alandia and Bergamont. Is Chiemera bound by the treaty? What obligations might it nonetheless have regarding the treaty, and how could it free itself from them? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — Chiemera never ratified, so it is not a party; as a signatory it must only refrain from acts that would defeat the object and purpose (Art 18(a)) until it clearly declares that it will not become a party.
• The treaty requires ratification (Art 14); signature is not consent → Chiemera is neither contracting State nor party; the treaty is res inter alios acta for it (Art 34).
• Art 18(a): duty of abstention only — e.g. not ruining the lake's tourist use by massive pollution or overfishing — not a duty to perform the treaty.
• Release: by making its intention clear not to become a party, e.g. by formal notification to the depositary Bergamont (cf. US 2002, Russia 2016 on the Rome Statute).
• Note: a Minister of Tourism is not an Art 7(2)(a) office; if he signed without full powers, the signature has no legal effect unless confirmed (Art 8) — then not even Art 18 applies.
Memorise: Signatory ≠ party · Art 18(a): do not defeat object and purpose · end it by a clear declaration to the depositary.

cards.q: State Xenia ratifies a multilateral convention with a reservation excluding Art 7 (compulsory dispute settlement). Yorvik expressly accepts the reservation; Zelan objects without further comment; Wendor objects and declares that the convention shall not enter into force between itself and Xenia; Valdo says nothing for 14 months after notification. What are the treaty relations between Xenia and each of these States, and among the four of them? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Xenia–Yorvik and Xenia–Valdo: convention in force without Art 7 (reciprocally); Xenia–Zelan: in force, but Art 7 does not apply between them; Xenia–Wendor: no treaty relations; among the others Art 7 applies unchanged.
• Yorvik: express acceptance (Art 20(4)(a)) → treaty relations; Art 7 excluded for Xenia and reciprocally for Yorvik towards Xenia (Art 21(1)).
• Valdo: no objection within 12 months = tacit acceptance (Art 20(5)) → as for Yorvik.
• Zelan: simple objection does not preclude entry into force (Art 20(4)(b)); Art 7 does not apply between Zelan and Xenia to the extent of the reservation (Art 21(3)) — for an excluding reservation the result equals acceptance.
• Wendor: qualified objection (contrary intention definitely expressed) → no treaty relations with Xenia (Art 20(4)(b)).
• Among Yorvik, Zelan, Wendor and Valdo Art 7 applies unchanged (Art 21(2)). Xenia's consent is effective because at least one State accepted (Art 20(4)(c)).
Memorise: Accept / 12 months' silence → modified relation · simple objection → minus provision · qualified → none · others untouched (21(2)).

cards.q: On 10 March 2025 the depositary notifies all States of a reservation made by State Rhos to a multilateral convention. State Quell has been a party since 2022; State Pira ratifies on 1 August 2025; State Sorn ratifies on 1 June 2026. Until when can each of them object before it is deemed to have accepted the reservation? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Quell and Pira until 10 March 2026; Sorn at the latest when it ratifies on 1 June 2026.
• Art 20(5): a reservation is considered accepted by a State if it has raised no objection by the end of 12 months after it was notified of the reservation or by the date on which it expressed its consent to be bound, whichever is later.
• Quell: notified 10 March 2025, consent earlier → 10 March 2026.
• Pira: 10 March 2026 is later than its consent (1 August 2025) → 10 March 2026.
• Sorn: consents only after the 12 months have run → the later date is its own consent: it must object together with its ratification, otherwise it has accepted.
• Objections must be in writing and communicated (Art 23(1)).
Memorise: Art 20(5) = the LATER of notification + 12 months and own consent.

cards.q: State Nadir ratifies a human rights convention with the reservation 'not to apply any provision of the Convention that is contrary to its national law'. Several States object that the reservation is incompatible with the object and purpose of the Convention. Is the reservation admissible, and what are the possible legal consequences of an impermissible reservation? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The reservation is inadmissible under Art 19(c); the VCLT does not settle the consequence — views range from Nadir not being a party at all to Nadir being bound without the benefit of the reservation (severability), which the ILC now presumes.
• Admissibility: a general reservation subordinating the whole treaty to national law is too vague to assess and removes the core obligations → incompatible with the object and purpose (Art 19(c); cf. Saudi Arabia's CEDAW reservation and Austria's objection).
• Consequences (disputed): (1) Nadir's consent is vitiated — it is not a party; (2) the reservation operates vis-à-vis accepting States and objections take effect under Art 20–21 (inter-State practice); (3) severability: the reservation is null and Nadir is bound by the whole treaty — ECtHR Belilos (1988), UN Human Rights Committee General Comment 24 (1994).
• ILC Guide to Practice on Reservations (2011): the author of an invalid reservation is presumed to be a party without the benefit of the reservation, unless it has expressed a contrary intention.
• Objections are not constitutive of invalidity but are evidence of it and part of the 'reservations dialogue'.
Memorise: Invalid (Art 19(c)) → not a party vs severance (Belilos, GC 24) · ILC 2011: party without the reservation unless contrary intention.

cards.q: In 2023 State Orlan signed a convention subject to ratification and attached a reservation to Art 12. When it ratified in 2025 it did not repeat the reservation. In 2026 it wants to make an additional reservation to Art 15. Assess both reservations. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Art 12 reservation lapsed because it was not confirmed upon ratification, and the Art 15 reservation comes too late — it is possible only if no other contracting State objects.
• Art 23(2): a reservation formulated when signing a treaty subject to ratification must be formally confirmed when the State expresses its consent to be bound; it is then considered made on the date of confirmation. Without confirmation it has no effect → Orlan is fully bound by Art 12.
• Art 19 chapeau: reservations may be formulated only when signing, ratifying, accepting, approving or acceding. A late reservation after consent is admissible only if none of the other contracting States objects (ILC Guide to Practice 2011; UN depositary practice) — otherwise Orlan stays bound by Art 15.
• Workarounds such as withdrawing and re-acceding with a reservation are controversial (Rawle Kennedy v Trinidad and Tobago, UN HRC 1999).
Memorise: Reservation at signature → confirm at ratification (Art 23(2)) · after consent → only if nobody objects.

cards.q: (1) Three States conclude a treaty establishing a joint regime for the dam on their shared river; one ratifies with a reservation. (2) A State accedes to the founding treaty of an international organization with a reservation. (3) A State that made a reservation ten years ago now wishes to withdraw it. Which special rules apply? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) acceptance by all parties may be required (Art 20(2)); (2) acceptance by the competent organ of the IO (Art 20(3)); (3) withdrawal is possible at any time and becomes operative upon notice (Art 22).
• (1) Art 20(2): where the limited number of negotiating States and the object and purpose show that application of the treaty in its entirety between all parties is an essential condition of each State's consent — typical for a three-State dam regime — a reservation needs acceptance by all parties (the old unanimity rule).
• (2) Art 20(3): unless otherwise provided, a reservation to a constituent instrument of an international organization requires the acceptance of the competent organ of that organization.
• (3) Art 22: unless the treaty provides otherwise, a reservation (and an objection) may be withdrawn at any time; the consent of accepting States is not required; the withdrawal becomes operative for another State when that State receives notice; in writing (Art 23(4)).
Memorise: 20(2) small group + integrity → all accept · 20(3) IO charter → organ accepts · Art 22 withdraw any time, effective on receipt.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'After its parliament has passed a new statute contradicting a treaty, a State may lawfully stop performing the treaty, because the later law prevails.' (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — pacta sunt servanda (Art 26) binds the State regardless of its domestic law, and internal law is no justification for non-performance (Art 27).
• Art 26: every treaty in force is binding upon the parties and must be performed by them in good faith.
• Art 27: a party may not invoke the provisions of its internal law — later statutes, even the constitution — as justification for its failure to perform. Lex posterior works only within one legal order, not between domestic and international law.
• Only exception (Art 27 second sentence → Art 46): a manifest violation of a fundamental internal rule on competence to conclude treaties — which concerns the conclusion, not later legislation.
• Consequence: non-performance is an internationally wrongful act → state responsibility. Lawful exit only via the treaty clause or Art 54 ff.
Memorise: Art 26 pacta sunt servanda + Art 27 internal law no excuse (except Art 46) · breach → responsibility.

cards.q: A convention against torture entered into force for State Mirel on 1 March 2020. A victim complains of (1) torture by Mirel's police in 2018 and (2) Mirel's refusal, since 2018 and still continuing, to investigate the torture. Can the convention be applied to these facts? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Not to the 2018 torture itself (Art 28), but possibly to the continuing failure to investigate for the period after 1 March 2020.
• Art 28: unless a different intention appears from the treaty or is otherwise established, its provisions do not bind a party in relation to any act or fact which took place, or any situation which ceased to exist, before the date of entry into force for that party.
• (1) Torture in 2018 = completed act before EIF → the convention does not apply (only custom and treaties then in force).
• (2) A situation that continues after EIF can be measured against the treaty from 1 March 2020 on (continuing omission).
• Distinguish Art 4: the VCLT itself applies only to treaties concluded after it entered into force for the States concerned.
Memorise: Art 28: completed acts before EIF out · continuing situations in from EIF · Art 4 = VCLT itself.

cards.q: In 2010 States A, B and C conclude a treaty on the transport of hazardous waste (Treaty I). In 2020 A and B — but not C — conclude Treaty II on the same subject with stricter rules incompatible with Treaty I. Neither treaty refers to the other. Which treaty governs the relations between A and B, and between A and C? What if an obligation under Treaty II conflicted with the UN Charter? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Between A and B Treaty II prevails as the later treaty (Treaty I applies only insofar as compatible); between A and C only Treaty I; Charter obligations would prevail over both (Art 103).
• Art 30(1)–(2): subject to Art 103 UN Charter; where a treaty states that it is subject to, or not incompatible with, another treaty, that other treaty prevails.
• Art 30(3): if all parties to the earlier treaty are also parties to the later one (and the earlier one is not terminated under Art 59), the earlier applies only to the extent compatible with the later (lex posterior).
• Art 30(4): not all parties identical — (a) between States party to both treaties: as in (3) → Treaty II prevails between A and B; (b) between a State party to both and a State party to only one: the treaty to which both are parties → Treaty I governs A–C and B–C.
• Art 30(5), Art 41: if Treaty II impairs C's rights under Treaty I, A and B are responsible towards C.
• Art 103 Charter: in a conflict, Charter obligations (incl. binding Security Council resolutions) prevail over obligations under any other international agreement.
Memorise: Art 103 Charter first · lex posterior among common parties (30(3), (4)(a)) · with outsiders the common treaty (30(4)(b)) · responsibility (30(5)).

cards.q: States Pora and Quin conclude a canal treaty. It grants all merchant ships of State Rin free passage and obliges State Sella, an upstream neighbour, to keep the water level constant. Rin's ships use the canal; Sella never reacts. Later Pora and Quin wish to abolish Rin's right of passage. What is the legal position of Rin and Sella? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Rin has acquired the right because its assent is presumed; Sella is not bound, because obligations for third States require express written acceptance; Rin's right may be revoked unless it was intended to be irrevocable.
• Art 34: pacta tertiis nec nocent nec prosunt — a treaty creates neither obligations nor rights for a third State without its consent.
• Rights (Art 36): arise if the parties intend to accord a right and the third State assents; assent is presumed as long as the contrary is not indicated. Rin's use confirms it; Rin must comply with the conditions for its exercise (Art 36(2)).
• Obligations (Art 35): only if the parties intend to create an obligation and the third State expressly accepts it in writing — Sella's silence is not enough → not bound.
• Revocation (Art 37): an obligation may be revoked or modified only with the consent of the parties and the third State; a right may not be revoked or modified if it was intended not to be revocable or modifiable without the third State's consent — otherwise Pora and Quin may abolish Rin's right.
• Treaty rules may bind third States as custom (Art 38); PCIJ Free Zones (1932): Art 435 Versailles did not bind Switzerland without its consent.
Memorise: Art 34 pacta tertiis · rights: assent presumed (36) · obligations: express + written (35) · revocation (37) · custom (38).

cards.q: Aldoam, Bertus, Cilco and Daroto are parties to the Rare Earth Materials Treaty (REMT), which aims to reduce the environmental impact of rare earth mining and contains no amendment clause. After a decade REMT has not proved as effective as hoped, so Aldoam and Daroto want to amend the treaty to ban rare earth mining outright. Bertus disagrees because its economy relies heavily on mining. Under what circumstances can a multilateral treaty be amended by some but not all parties, and what are the effects of such an amendment? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: A formal amendment must be open to all parties and binds only those who accept it (Art 39–40); Aldoam and Daroto alone may modify REMT between themselves only under Art 41 — either way the original REMT continues to govern their relations with Bertus (and with Cilco, unless it joins).
• Art 39: amendment by agreement between the parties; the treaty's own amendment rules prevail (none here). Amendment is distinct from inter se modification.
• Art 40: every proposal must be notified to all contracting States, each of which may take part in the decision and in negotiating the amending agreement — Bertus and Cilco cannot be excluded. The amending agreement does not bind a party that does not become party to it (Art 40(4), Art 30(4)(b)); States joining later are parties to the amended treaty towards those bound by it and to the old one towards the others (Art 40(5)).
• Art 41 inter se modification: permissible if (a) provided for by the treaty, or (b) not prohibited and (i) it does not affect the enjoyment by the other parties of their rights or the performance of their obligations, and (ii) it does not relate to a provision derogation from which is incompatible with the effective execution of the object and purpose; the other parties must be notified (Art 41(2)).
• Application: a ban limited to Aldoam's and Daroto's territories pursues REMT's aim of reducing environmental harm, so it is hardly incompatible with the object and purpose; it is unlawful, however, if it affects Bertus's rights under REMT (e.g. guaranteed access to mining or trade in rare earths).
• Effects: between Aldoam and Daroto the modified rules prevail (lex posterior, Art 30(4)(a)); with Bertus (and Cilco) the unchanged REMT applies (Art 30(4)(b), Art 34). A modification breaching Art 41 → responsibility towards Bertus (Art 30(5)).
Memorise: Amend = all may participate, binds only acceptors (39–40) · inter se = Art 41: allowed/not prohibited + no effect on others + object and purpose + notify · effects Art 30(4).

cards.q: Distinguish revision, amendment and modification of a treaty, and give examples of treaty-specific amendment procedures. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Amendment is a formal change intended for all parties (Art 39–40), modification an inter se change between some parties only (Art 41), and revision the traditional term for a comprehensive re-working of a treaty.
• Amendment (Art 39–40): by agreement; all contracting States are notified and may participate; binds only States that become party to the amending agreement — unless the treaty provides otherwise, e.g. Art 108 UN Charter: amendments adopted by two thirds of the General Assembly and ratified by two thirds of Members including all permanent members bind all Members.
• Modification (Art 41): agreement between certain parties altering the treaty in their mutual relations only; allowed if provided for or not prohibited, without prejudice to the others and compatible with object and purpose.
• Revision: comprehensive overhaul, e.g. a general review conference under Art 109 UN Charter — legally subject to the amendment rules.
• Informal change is also possible through subsequent practice (Art 31(3)(b)).
Memorise: Amendment = all (39–40) · modification = inter se (41) · revision = overhaul (Art 109 Charter) · Art 108 Charter binds all.

cards.q: Under which conditions can the validity of a treaty be challenged? Distinguish relative from absolute grounds of invalidity. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only on the exhaustive grounds of Art 46–53 VCLT (Art 42); relative grounds (Art 46–50) must be invoked by the affected State and can be lost, absolute grounds (Art 51–53) render the treaty void.
• Art 42(1): the validity of a treaty or of consent may be impeached only through the application of the Convention.
• Relative grounds (defects of consent): Art 46 manifest violation of an internal rule of fundamental importance on competence; Art 47 disregard of a specific restriction on authority notified in advance; Art 48 error concerning a fact or situation forming an essential basis of consent; Art 49 fraud by another negotiating State; Art 50 corruption of the representative by another negotiating State.
• Absolute grounds: Art 51 coercion of the representative ('without any legal effect'); Art 52 coercion of the State by the threat or use of force contrary to the Charter; Art 53 conflict with ius cogens at the time of conclusion.
• Consequences: relative — invoked only by the injured State, lost by express agreement or acquiescence (Art 45), separability possible (Art 44(3)–(4)); absolute — no loss of right, no separability (Art 44(5)); effects Art 69, 71; procedure Art 65–67. A conflict with ordinary domestic law is no ground (Art 27).
Memorise: Relative 46–50 (competence, authority, error, fraud, corruption) → invoke, Art 45 · absolute 51–53 (coercion ×2, ius cogens) → void, no separation.

cards.q: (1) Tarsis instructed its negotiator not to accept an arbitration clause, but did not inform the other side; the negotiator signed a treaty containing the clause, consent being expressed by signature. (2) Ulmar concluded a boundary treaty with an annexed map; years later it discovers that the map shows a line different from what it believed the text described, although its own experts had examined the map at the time. Can Tarsis and Ulmar invoke the invalidity of their consent? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No in both cases — Tarsis's restriction was not notified beforehand (Art 47), and Ulmar cannot plead error because it contributed to it and was on notice (Art 48(2), Temple of Preah Vihear).
• Art 47: if a representative's authority was subject to a specific restriction, its disregard may be invoked only if the restriction was notified to the other negotiating States before he expressed consent. Internal instructions only → Tarsis is bound.
• Art 48(1): error invalidates consent if it relates to a fact or situation assumed to exist at the time of conclusion and forming an essential basis of consent. Art 48(2): not if the State contributed to the error by its own conduct or the circumstances put it on notice of a possible error.
• ICJ, Temple of Preah Vihear (1962): Thailand could not plead error about the map it had received, accepted and used and whose error it could have detected. Ulmar's experts examined the map → on notice.
• In addition, long acceptance = acquiescence (Art 45(b)); mere errors in the wording → correction (Art 79).
Memorise: Restriction on authority counts only if notified in advance (47) · error: essential basis, not self-caused, not on notice (48, Preah Vihear) · Art 45.

cards.q: Assess the validity of the following treaties: (1) State Varn's President signs a treaty ceding territory after being threatened, during night-time negotiations, with arrest and with the bombing of his capital; (2) State Wolde accepts a trade treaty after its neighbour threatens to cut off all imports; (3) Xandor's negotiator agreed to a treaty after receiving a large payment from the other negotiating State. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) void — coercion of the representative and of the State (Art 51, 52); (2) not void under Art 52, as economic pressure is not 'force'; (3) voidable at Xandor's instance for corruption (Art 50).
• (1) Art 51: consent procured by coercion of the representative through acts or threats directed against him is without any legal effect (Hácha, Berlin, March 1939). Art 52: a treaty procured by the threat or use of force in violation of the principles of the UN Charter (Art 2(4)) is void — threatening to bomb the capital coerces the State. Absolute grounds: no validation (Art 45 inapplicable), no separability (Art 44(5)).
• (2) 'Force' in Art 52 means armed force; attempts to include economic and political pressure failed at the Vienna Conference (only a non-binding declaration condemning such coercion). The pressure may violate non-intervention, but the treaty is not void under Art 52.
• (3) Art 50: corruption of the representative directly or indirectly by another negotiating State allows Xandor to invoke invalidity (relative ground; similarly fraud, Art 49). It must do so by notification (Art 65) and may lose the right by acquiescence (Art 45); the corrupting State cannot rely on Art 69(2) (Art 69(3)).
Memorise: Coerce the person (51) / the State by force (52) → void · economic pressure ≠ Art 52 · fraud (49) / corruption (50) → relative.

cards.q: (1) In 2024 States Arbon and Belos conclude a treaty on the joint deportation and enslavement of an ethnic minority. (2) A treaty from 1930 permits a practice that is prohibited by a peremptory norm which emerged later. What is the fate of the two treaties? (2 points)
cards.a:
