Short answer: The 2024 treaty is void from the outset (Art 53); the 1930 treaty becomes void and terminates from the emergence of the new peremptory norm (Art 64).
• Ius cogens (Art 53): a norm accepted and recognized by the international community of States as a whole as non-derogable, modifiable only by a later norm of the same character — e.g. prohibitions of genocide, slavery, torture, apartheid.
• (1) Conflict at conclusion → void ab initio, as a whole (Art 44(5)); the parties must eliminate the consequences of acts performed under it and bring their relations into conformity (Art 71(1)); Art 45 inapplicable.
• (2) Art 64: a new peremptory norm renders an existing conflicting treaty void and it terminates — ex nunc: rights created before survive only insofar as their maintenance does not conflict with the new norm (Art 71(2)).
• Disputes on Art 53/64 can be brought to the ICJ by application (Art 66(a)).
Memorise: Art 53 = void from the start (71(1): undo) · Art 64 = void from now on (71(2)) · no separation, no acquiescence · ICJ (66(a)).

cards.q: In 2008 State Corvo discovered that it had concluded a fisheries treaty in 2005 on the basis of a fundamental error of fact. It nevertheless kept performing the treaty and accepting payments under it until 2025, when it claimed invalidity. Assess, and state whether the same would apply to a claim that the treaty had been imposed by the threat of force. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Corvo has lost the right to invoke the error by acquiescence (Art 45(b)); the loss-of-right rule does not apply to coercion or ius cogens.
• Art 45: a State may no longer invoke a ground for invalidating, terminating, withdrawing from or suspending a treaty under Art 46–50 or Art 60 and 62 if, after becoming aware of the facts, it (a) expressly agreed that the treaty is valid or remains in force, or (b) by its conduct must be considered as having acquiesced in its validity or its maintenance in force.
• Corvo knew since 2008 and performed for 17 years, even accepting benefits → acquiescence → error (Art 48) is no longer available (cf. Temple of Preah Vihear).
• Coercion (Art 51, 52) and ius cogens (Art 53, 64) are not listed in Art 45 — a void treaty cannot be validated by conduct.
Memorise: Art 45 = knowledge + express agreement or acquiescence → right lost · only for 46–50, 60, 62 · not for 51–53, 64.

cards.q: Astamor, Balala and Cumo are bound by several agreements concerning lead in the groundwater of the Xympora Peninsula, e.g. the 1956 Investigation Convention (Astamor–Balala), whose purpose seems largely achieved since a purification process was invented in 1994, and the 1996 Debt Allocation Agreement. Under what conditions does a State have the right to terminate a treaty? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: A State may terminate or withdraw in accordance with the treaty, by consent of all parties, where a right is implied (Art 56), or on the grounds of material breach, supervening impossibility, fundamental change of circumstances or new ius cogens — following the procedure of Art 65–67.
• Treaty provisions (Art 54(a)): termination/withdrawal clause with notice periods (Paris Agreement Art 28: after 3 years, effective 1 year after notification; Austria–Kuwait BIT: notice 1 year before the end of a 30-year period, 20-year survival clause).
• Consent (Art 54(b)): at any time by consent of all parties after consultation; also a later treaty on the same subject by all parties (Art 59).
• No clause (Art 56): only if the parties intended to allow it or a right is implied by the nature of the treaty (e.g. commercial treaties, alliances; not boundary or human rights treaties); 12 months' notice.
• Material breach by another party (Art 60): repudiation or violation of a provision essential to the object or purpose; bilateral → terminate or suspend; multilateral → unanimous decision of the others, suspension by a specially affected party, or by any party for integral treaties; not humanitarian protections (Art 60(5)).
• Supervening impossibility (Art 61): permanent disappearance or destruction of an object indispensable for execution (temporary → suspension), not self-caused.
• Fundamental change of circumstances (Art 62): the circumstances were an essential basis of consent, the change was unforeseen and radically transforms the obligations still to be performed; excluded for boundaries and self-caused change (Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997: very restrictive).
• New peremptory norm (Art 64) → treaty void and terminates. Not grounds: severance of diplomatic relations (Art 63, unless indispensable), fall of the number of parties below the EIF threshold (Art 55). Desuetude only by conduct of all parties.
• Procedure: written notification with reasons, at least three months' waiting period, dispute settlement if objection (Art 65–67); in principle the whole treaty (Art 44); right lost by acquiescence for Art 60 and 62 (Art 45).
• Xympora: that the lead problem is solved does not by itself terminate the 1956 Convention — Astamor needs its clause, Balala's consent (Art 54(b)) or, exceptionally, Art 62; as a pre-1980 treaty it is governed by the corresponding customary rules (Art 4).
Memorise: Treaty (54(a)) → consent (54(b), 59) → implied right (56) → breach (60) / impossibility (61) / rebus (62) / ius cogens (64) · procedure 65–67 · Art 45.

cards.q: Astamor, Balala and Cumo consider ending or pausing some of their agreements on lead in the Xympora groundwater. How do the invalidity, termination and suspension of a treaty differ in their effects? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Invalidity makes the treaty void from the outset (ex tunc), termination ends obligations for the future (ex nunc) leaving past execution intact, and suspension merely pauses performance.
• Invalidity (Art 69): the treaty is void and its provisions have no legal force; where acts were performed in reliance, each party may require the others to restore as far as possible the position that would have existed; acts performed in good faith before invalidity was invoked are not unlawful by reason only of the invalidity — not for the party responsible for fraud, corruption or coercion (Art 69(3)). Ius cogens: eliminate consequences (Art 71(1)).
• Termination (Art 70): releases the parties from further performance; does not affect rights, obligations or legal situations created through its execution before termination; withdrawal has this effect for the withdrawing State.
• Suspension (Art 72): releases the parties from performance during the suspension only; the legal relations otherwise continue and the parties must refrain from acts tending to obstruct resumption.
Memorise: Invalid = void ab initio, restore (69) · terminate = ex nunc, past stays (70) · suspend = pause, do not obstruct resumption (72).

cards.q: Following a change of government in State X, the newly elected President announces her intention to withdraw from all bilateral and multilateral treaties aimed at protecting the environment, the climate and biodiversity. She instructs her cabinet members to submit proposals on how State X could achieve this, if possible in accordance with international law. Give 5 proposals that cabinet members well versed in international law could submit. Supplement them with an assessment of their prospects of success and distinguish which would be relatively easy to implement, which difficult, and which would have little chance of success. (10 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Easy: withdraw under the treaties' own withdrawal/termination clauses; difficult: termination by consent, withdrawal from treaties without a clause (Art 56), amendment or withdrawal-and-reaccession; little chance: material breach, impossibility, fundamental change of circumstances or invalidity — and simply stopping performance would be a breach.
Starting point: pacta sunt servanda (Art 26 VCLT); a change of government does not affect the State's identity or its treaty obligations; internal politics are no excuse (Art 27). A lawful exit must use Part V VCLT (or the corresponding custom).
• 1. Withdrawal under the treaty's clause (Art 54(a)) — EASY. Most environmental treaties contain one, e.g. Paris Agreement Art 28: written notification to the depositary at any time after 3 years from its entry into force for the party, effective 1 year after receipt (used by the USA in 2019/2020 and again in 2025); UNFCCC and CBD are similar. Bilateral treaties: termination clause with notice. Respect notice periods; the instrument must be signed by the Head of State, Head of Government or Foreign Minister or come with full powers (Art 67(2)) — the President can sign herself.
• 2. Termination by consent of all parties (Art 54(b); suspension Art 57(b); replacement by a later treaty Art 59) — always legally possible, but requires every partner's agreement: for bilateral treaties DIFFICULT but negotiable; for multilateral treaties with almost 200 parties practically hopeless.
• 3. Treaties without a withdrawal clause (Art 56) — DIFFICULT: allowed only if the parties intended it or the nature of the treaty implies it, with 12 months' notice; for common-interest treaties protecting the environment an implied right is doubtful (cf. HRC General Comment 26 on human rights treaties).
• 4. Material breach by another party (Art 60) — LITTLE CHANCE: requires a repudiation or violation of an essential provision by a specific party; in multilateral treaties only unanimous action of the others, suspension by a specially affected party, or integral treaties (Art 60(2)); it cannot serve as a pretext, and a premature reaction is itself unlawful (Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997).
• 5. Fundamental change of circumstances (Art 62) — LITTLE CHANCE: a new government's policy or higher costs are not a change of an essential basis radically transforming the obligations; the ICJ applies Art 62 very restrictively (Fisheries Jurisdiction 1973, Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997). Supervening impossibility (Art 61) also fails: the environment as object has not disappeared.
• Further options: invalidity (Art 46–53) — LITTLE CHANCE: disagreement is no ground; only e.g. a manifest violation of a fundamental rule on competence (Art 46), and long performance amounts to acquiescence (Art 45). Amendment (Art 39–40) or inter se suspension (Art 58) — DIFFICULT: needs others' agreement; X is not bound by amendments it rejects but cannot impose weaker rules. Withdrawal and immediate re-accession with reservations — DIFFICULT/controversial: reservations must still pass Art 19(c) and the manoeuvre may be abusive (Rawle Kennedy, HRC 1999).
• Simply ceasing to perform is not in accordance with international law: an internationally wrongful act entailing state responsibility (reparation, countermeasures by injured States).
• Procedure for grounds outside the treaty clause: written notification with reasons, at least 3 months' waiting period, peaceful settlement if another party objects (Art 65–67); withdrawal in principle only from the whole treaty (Art 44).
• Limit: even after withdrawal X remains bound by customary environmental law — no-harm/prevention principle, duty to conduct an environmental impact assessment (Pulp Mills 2010) — Art 43 VCLT.
Memorise: EASY = treaty clause (54(a)) · DIFFICULT = consent (54(b), 59), Art 56, amendment/re-accession · LITTLE CHANCE = 60, 61, 62, 46–53 · procedure 65–67 · custom stays (Art 43).

cards.q: A bilateral investment treaty between Teral and Umbria entered into force on 1 March 1996. It runs for 30 years and is renewed automatically for further 30-year periods unless a party gives written notice at least one year before the expiry of a period; for investments made before termination takes effect it continues to apply for another 20 years. Teral sends notice of termination on 15 June 2025. When does the treaty end, and until when can an investor who invested in 2010 rely on it? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The notice is too late for the first period (ending 1 March 2026), so the treaty is renewed and ends at the earliest on 1 March 2056; thanks to the survival clause the 2010 investor is protected until 1 March 2076.
• Route: termination in conformity with the treaty (Art 54(a)) — read the final clauses first.
• First period: 1 March 1996 – 1 March 2026; notice needed by 1 March 2025. The notice of 15 June 2025 does not meet the one-year deadline → automatic renewal until 2056; the notice can take effect at the end of that period (if it is treated as notice for the next expiry; otherwise it must be repeated in time).
• Survival clause: investments made before termination remain protected for 20 more years → until 2076.
• Earlier exit only by agreement with Umbria (Art 54(b)) or on the grounds of Art 60–62.
Memorise: Final clause decides · late notice → renewal · survival clause adds 20 years.

cards.q: State Ferran wants to withdraw from (1) the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, (2) a bilateral boundary treaty, and (3) a bilateral treaty of commerce and navigation. None of them contains a provision on denunciation or withdrawal. Is withdrawal possible? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Not from the ICCPR or the boundary treaty; probably yes from the commercial treaty, with at least 12 months' notice (Art 56).
• Art 56(1): a treaty without a provision on termination, denunciation or withdrawal is not subject to them unless (a) it is established that the parties intended to admit that possibility, or (b) a right may be implied by the nature of the treaty. Art 56(2): at least 12 months' notice.
• (1) ICCPR: human rights treaty, deliberately without a clause (unlike its First Optional Protocol); UN Human Rights Committee General Comment 26 (1997), after North Korea's attempted withdrawal: no denunciation — the rights belong to the people.
• (2) Boundary treaty: designed to create permanent, stable situations; no implied right (cf. Art 62(2)(a)); the boundary would survive anyway.
• (3) Commercial treaties (like alliances) are typically of a nature implying a right of denunciation → Ferran may withdraw with 12 months' written notice (Art 65, 67).
• Always possible: withdrawal with the consent of all parties (Art 54(b)).
Memorise: Silent treaty → no exit unless intended or implied by nature (56) · 12 months · commerce/alliances yes, boundaries/human rights no.

cards.q: (1) Under a bilateral water treaty, State Ilo diverts the shared river contrary to the treaty's central provision. (2) Under a multilateral fisheries treaty with 20 parties, State Jura massively exceeds its catch quota in waters bordering State Kiva. (3) Under a multilateral disarmament treaty, State Lorn openly produces prohibited weapons. What rights do the other parties have? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) the other party may terminate or suspend the treaty; (2) specially affected Kiva may suspend it towards Jura (termination needs a unanimous decision of the others); (3) any party may suspend the treaty for itself, because the breach radically changes every party's position.
• Material breach (Art 60(3)): (a) repudiation not sanctioned by the VCLT, or (b) violation of a provision essential to the accomplishment of the object or purpose. Minor breaches → only state responsibility and countermeasures.
• (1) Bilateral (Art 60(1)): the other party may invoke the breach as a ground for terminating the treaty or suspending it in whole or in part — diverting the river against the central provision is material.
• (2) Multilateral (Art 60(2)): (a) the other parties by unanimous agreement may suspend or terminate the treaty either between themselves and Jura or among all parties; (b) a party specially affected (Kiva) may suspend it in whole or in part between itself and Jura. Quotas are essential to a fisheries regime → material.
• (3) Art 60(2)(c): for treaties of such a character that a material breach radically changes the position of every party with respect to further performance (integral treaties, e.g. disarmament), any party other than the defaulting State may suspend the treaty with respect to itself.
• Limits: not for provisions protecting the human person in treaties of a humanitarian character (Art 60(5)); special treaty regimes prevail (Art 60(4)); procedure Art 65–67; no premature reaction (Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997: Hungary's 1992 termination preceded the breach); acquiescence (Art 45). Namibia AO (1971): mandate terminated for material breach.
Memorise: Material = repudiation or essential provision (60(3)) · bilateral: terminate/suspend · multilateral: others unanimously / specially affected suspends / integral: any suspends · 60(5) humanitarian excluded.

cards.q: (1) An island that two States agreed to administer jointly disappears permanently after a volcanic eruption. (2) A dam jointly operated under a treaty is temporarily damaged by an earthquake. (3) State Mora deliberately drains a lake that was the object of a fishing treaty. Can the treaties be terminated for supervening impossibility of performance? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) yes, termination; (2) only suspension while the dam is out of operation; (3) no — Mora cannot rely on an impossibility it caused itself.
• Art 61(1): impossibility may be invoked as a ground for terminating or withdrawing if it results from the permanent disappearance or destruction of an object indispensable for the execution of the treaty; if the impossibility is temporary, only as a ground for suspension.
• Art 61(2): not if the impossibility results from a breach by the invoking party of a treaty obligation or of any other international obligation owed to any other party.
• Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (1997): Hungary failed under Art 61 — the joint investment regime had not disappeared and Hungary had itself contributed; financial difficulties do not create impossibility.
• Procedure Art 65–67.
Memorise: Art 61: permanent loss of an indispensable object → terminate · temporary → suspend · self-caused → excluded.

cards.q: Twenty years after concluding a treaty with Ostrava on a joint hydroelectric project, which also fixes the common border along the river, State Nevra argues that (1) the fall of its former regime, (2) the reduced economic profitability of the project and (3) new scientific knowledge about its environmental risks amount to a fundamental change of circumstances entitling it to terminate the whole treaty. Assess. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The argument fails: none of these changes affects an essential basis of consent in a way that radically transforms the obligations still to be performed, and the boundary part is excluded altogether (Art 62).
• Art 62(1): an unforeseen fundamental change of circumstances may be invoked only if (a) the existence of those circumstances constituted an essential basis of the parties' consent, and (b) the change radically transforms the extent of obligations still to be performed.
• Art 62(2): not if (a) the treaty establishes a boundary, or (b) the change results from a breach by the invoking party. Art 62(3): it may be invoked for suspension instead.
• Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (1997): the ICJ rejected exactly these arguments — political changes, diminished economic viability and progress of environmental knowledge were not unforeseen changes radically transforming the obligations; the stability of treaty relations requires applying Art 62 only in exceptional cases. See also Fisheries Jurisdiction (1973).
• Boundary part: excluded (Art 62(2)(a)); in any case the ground could at most affect separable clauses (Art 44(3)).
• Rare success: ECJ, Racke (1998) — suspension of the EC–Yugoslavia cooperation agreement during the war.
Memorise: Rebus (62) = essential basis + unforeseen + radical transformation · not boundaries, not self-caused · Gabčíkovo: politics, economics, environment ≠ enough.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statements? Give reasons. (1) 'When two States break off diplomatic relations, all treaties between them terminate.' (2) 'When the number of parties to a multilateral treaty falls below the number required for its entry into force, the treaty terminates.' (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both statements are wrong (Art 63 and Art 55 VCLT).
• (1) Art 63: the severance of diplomatic or consular relations does not affect the legal relations established by a treaty, except insofar as the existence of such relations is indispensable for its application (e.g. treaty provisions working through the diplomatic missions). Breaking off relations is a lawful unfriendly act (retorsion), not a termination ground.
• (2) Art 55: unless the treaty otherwise provides, a multilateral treaty does not terminate by reason only of the fact that the number of parties falls below the number necessary for its entry into force — the threshold governs only the beginning.
• Related: one party's withdrawal from a multilateral treaty leaves it in force for the rest; in a bilateral treaty it terminates the treaty.
Memorise: Art 63: no diplomatic relations ≠ termination (unless indispensable) · Art 55: falling below the threshold ≠ termination.

cards.q: State Orsk wants to terminate a multilateral treaty, invoking a fundamental change of circumstances. Which procedure must it follow, and what happens if another party objects? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Orsk must notify the other parties in writing with reasons, wait at least three months and, if an objection is raised, seek a peaceful settlement — failing which within 12 months, compulsory conciliation under the VCLT Annex (the ICJ only for ius cogens disputes).
• Art 65(1): the party invoking a ground for invalidity, termination, withdrawal or suspension must notify the other parties of its claim, the measure proposed and the reasons.
• Art 65(2): if after a period of not less than three months (except in cases of special urgency) no party has objected, it may carry out the measure by an instrument under Art 67.
• Art 65(3): if an objection is raised, the parties must seek a solution through the means listed in Art 33 UN Charter (negotiation, mediation, arbitration, judicial settlement …).
• Art 66: no solution within 12 months → disputes on Art 53/64 may be submitted to the ICJ by application (unless arbitration is agreed); other Part V disputes → conciliation commission (Annex, request to the UN Secretary-General), non-binding report.
• Art 67: notification in writing; the instrument must be signed by the Head of State, Head of Government or Foreign Minister, otherwise full powers may be requested. Art 68: revocable until it takes effect.
• Also: in principle only the whole treaty (Art 44); right lost if Orsk had acquiesced (Art 45).
Memorise: Notify with reasons (65) → 3 months → objection → Art 33 Charter → 12 months → ICJ (ius cogens) / conciliation (66) → instrument (67).

cards.q: State X wants to (1) get rid of a bilateral nature-protection treaty with its neighbour Y that contains no termination clause, and (2) escape the core obligation of a multilateral biodiversity protocol while remaining a party, by withdrawing under the protocol's clause and immediately re-acceding with a reservation excluding that obligation. Assess both routes. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) Possible at any time with Y's consent (Art 54(b)), otherwise hardly (Art 56); (2) the withdrawal is lawful, but the reservation would be inadmissible as contrary to the object and purpose and the manoeuvre is likely abusive.
• (1) Art 54(b): termination at any time by consent of all parties (bilateral: X and Y), also by concluding a new treaty replacing it (Art 59). Unilaterally only if a right is intended or implied by its nature (Art 56) — doubtful for a nature-protection treaty — with 12 months' notice.
• (2) Withdrawal under the clause is lawful (Art 54(a)). A reservation on re-accession must meet Art 19: excluding the core obligation is incompatible with the object and purpose (Art 19(c)); other parties may object. The denunciation–re-accession technique circumvents the rule that reservations may only be made at the time of consent and may violate good faith (UN Human Rights Committee, Rawle Kennedy v Trinidad and Tobago 1999: reservation invalid).
Memorise: Bilateral exit = agreement (54(b), 59) · re-accession with a reservation still subject to Art 19(c) + good faith.

cards.q: Two of the ten parties to a multilateral convention on river pollution want to suspend the convention between themselves alone for three years in order to test a new joint regime. Is this possible, and under what conditions? What is the effect of a suspension? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes, under Art 58 — if the convention provides for it or does not prohibit it, it does not affect the other parties' rights or obligations and it is compatible with the object and purpose; the other parties must be notified.
• Suspension of the whole treaty or of particular provisions: in conformity with the treaty or at any time by consent of all parties after consultation (Art 57).
• Art 58(1): two or more parties may suspend provisions temporarily and as between themselves alone if (a) the treaty provides for this, or (b) it is not prohibited and (i) does not affect the enjoyment of rights or the performance of obligations by the other parties and (ii) is not incompatible with the object and purpose. Art 58(2): notify the others.
• Application: if the two are upstream States, more pollution downstream would affect the other parties' rights → impermissible.
• Effect (Art 72): release from performance during the suspension only; the parties must not obstruct resumption.
Memorise: Suspension: treaty / all parties (57) · inter se (58) = Art 41-type conditions + notify · effect Art 72.

cards.q: State Galen signed, subject to ratification, a convention prohibiting the export of important cultural property; the convention needs 30 ratifications. (1) Before ratifying, Galen sells its most important national collection to a foreign museum. (2) State Hosta ratified in 2015, but by 2026 only 3 of the 30 ratifications have been deposited; it now adopts legislation contrary to the convention. (3) How can Galen end its interim obligation? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) The sale probably violates Art 18(a) because it defeats the object and purpose; (2) after eleven years with 3 of 30 ratifications entry into force is arguably 'unduly delayed', so Art 18(b) no longer binds Hosta; (3) Galen can free itself by clearly declaring that it will not become a party.
• Art 18: a State must refrain from acts which would defeat the object and purpose of a treaty when (a) it has signed subject to ratification, until it has made clear its intention not to become a party; or (b) it has expressed consent to be bound, pending entry into force and provided that entry into force is not unduly delayed.
• Only a duty of abstention: measures contrary to individual provisions are allowed; forbidden are acts that would render the treaty pointless or its later performance impossible. Selling the very collection the convention is meant to keep → defeat of object and purpose.
• (2) The Art 18(b) duty lapses when entry into force is unduly delayed — strongly arguable after 11 years with only a tenth of the ratifications.
• (3) A clear statement, e.g. notification to the depositary (USA and Israel 2002, Russia 2016 on the Rome Statute).
Memorise: Art 18 = abstain from defeating object and purpose · (a) signatory until clear 'no' · (b) ratifier until EIF, unless unduly delayed.

cards.q: A convention on the protection of glaciers provides: 'This Convention shall enter into force on the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the fifth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession. For each State ratifying, accepting, approving or acceding after the deposit of the fifth instrument, it shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the deposit by such State of its instrument.' Deposits: State 1 on 12.01.2027, State 2 on 03.03.2027, State 3 on 30.06.2027, State 4 (acceptance) on 01.12.2027, State 5 (accession) on 15.12.2027, State 6 on 10.02.2028, State 7 on 20.07.2028. Determine the objective entry into force and the entry into force for States 2, 6 and 7. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Objective entry into force on 14.03.2028 (also for States 1–5); for State 6 likewise on 14.03.2028, not earlier; for State 7 on 19.08.2028.
• Threshold: the 5th instrument is State 5's accession of 15.12.2027 — acceptance and accession count, as the clause says (Art 2(1)(b)).
• 90th day after 15.12.2027: 16 days of December (16–31) + 31 of January + 29 of February 2028 (leap year) = 76 → 14 more → 14.03.2028 = objective EIF.
• State 2 (like 1, 3, 4, 5): deposited earlier → bound from 14.03.2028.
• State 6: deposited after the fifth instrument; its 30th day would be 11.03.2028 — before the convention is in force at all. A treaty cannot enter into force for one State before it enters into force as such (Art 24(1), (3)) → 14.03.2028.
• State 7: 30th day after 20.07.2028 → 11 days of July + 19 of August → 19.08.2028.
Memorise: Count the n-th deposit (accessions count) · count from the day after deposit · watch leap years · no subjective EIF before the objective EIF.

cards.q: Four States P, Q, R and S negotiate and sign a treaty on a joint railway line. The treaty states that it 'shall be ratified' but contains no clause on entry into force, and nothing else was agreed. P, Q and R ratify in 2025; S announces that it will never ratify. Has the treaty entered into force? What can P, Q and R do? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — without a clause the treaty enters into force only once all negotiating States have consented (Art 24(2)); P, Q and R need an agreement on a different rule, a new treaty, or provisional application.
• Art 24(1): entry into force as provided or as the negotiating States agree — nothing here.
• Art 24(2): failing that, as soon as consent to be bound has been established for all the negotiating States → S's refusal blocks entry into force for everyone.
• Options: (a) an agreement of the negotiating States on another rule (Art 24(1)); (b) P, Q and R conclude a new treaty among themselves; (c) provisional application pending entry into force, if agreed (Art 25).
• S's Art 18 duty ends with its clear declaration.
Memorise: No EIF clause → all negotiating States (24(2)) · workarounds: agreement, new treaty, provisional application (25).

cards.q: A maritime safety convention enters into force 'twelve months after the date on which not less than five States, the combined merchant fleets of which constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping, have ratified it'; for States ratifying after its entry into force, 'three months after the deposit of their instrument'. Ratifications (share of world tonnage): Liberon (18 %) 02.02.2026, Pananova (15 %) 20.05.2026, Marsh (9 %) 01.09.2026, Grecia (4 %) 10.10.2026, Maltara (2 %) 30.11.2026, Singara (3 %) 15.01.2027, Tuvo (0.5 %) 01.12.2028. When does the convention enter into force, and when for Tuvo? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both conditions are first met on 15.01.2027 → objective entry into force on 15.01.2028; for Tuvo on 01.03.2029.
• Double threshold (cf. Paris Agreement Art 21: 55 parties and 55 % of emissions): the number of States and the tonnage share must both be reached.
• 30.11.2026: five States, but only 18 + 15 + 9 + 4 + 2 = 48 % → not yet.
• 15.01.2027: Singara adds 3 % → six States, 51 % → both conditions met → twelve months later = 15.01.2028 (for all six).
• Tuvo ratifies on 01.12.2028, after entry into force → three months → 01.03.2029 (Art 24(3)).
• Trap: taking the fifth ratification (30.11.2026) and computing 30.11.2027 ignores the tonnage condition.
Memorise: Double threshold = both conditions on the same day · then waiting period · later joiners: their own period.

cards.q: An agreement between Austria and Slovenia provides: 'This Agreement shall enter into force on the first day of the second month following the month in which the Contracting Parties have notified each other through diplomatic channels that their internal requirements for its entry into force have been fulfilled.' Austria notifies on 14.11.2026, Slovenia on 03.01.2027. When does the agreement enter into force, and what is the function of the notifications? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: On 01.03.2027 — the decisive month is January 2027 (month of the later notification), and the second month following it is March.
• Art 24(1): entry into force as the treaty provides; in bilateral treaties consent is typically established by exchange or mutual notification (Art 13, 16).
• Both notifications are required; the later one (03.01.2027) completes them → month: January → first following month February, second March → 01.03.2027.
• The notification is each State's international expression of consent after its domestic procedure (in Austria e.g. Nationalrat approval under Art 50 B-VG); domestic applicability in Austria follows from publication in BGBl III.
Memorise: 'Month in which both have notified' → count whole months after that month → first day.

cards.q: Aldoam, Bertus, Cilco and Daroto are parties to the Rare Earth Materials Treaty (REMT), which aims to reduce the environmental impact of rare earth mining. Six years after Aldoam and Daroto's attempt to amend REMT, Austria seeks to accede to it. What steps must the Austrian government take for the treaty to become law under Article 50 B-VG? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Federal Government must submit REMT to the Nationalrat for approval (Art 50(1) B-VG) with Bundesrat participation, have the Federal President issue the instrument of accession, deposit it, and publish the treaty in the BGBl III.
• Precondition: REMT must be open to accession, or the parties must agree (Art 15 VCLT).
• REMT amends/supplements domestic (mining and environmental) law and may be political → approval of the Nationalrat (Art 50(1) no. 1 B-VG) on a government bill.
• Bundesrat: consent required if the treaty regulates matters within the Länder's autonomous competence (Art 50(2) B-VG, e.g. nature protection).
• Possible Erfüllungsvorbehalt (Art 50(2) B-VG): implementation by laws before domestic application.
• Federal President signs the instrument of accession (Art 65(1) B-VG) on the Government's proposal, countersigned by the Federal Chancellor (Art 67 B-VG); deposit → consent established (Art 15–16 VCLT); entry into force for Austria per REMT (Art 24(3)).
• Publication by the Federal Chancellor in the Bundesgesetzblatt III (Art 49 B-VG) → domestic applicability.
Memorise: Govt bill → Nationalrat approval (50(1)) → Bundesrat (Länder!) → [Erfüllungsvorbehalt] → Federal President + countersignature (65, 67) → deposit → BGBl III (49).

cards.q: Describe the Austrian procedure for concluding a treaty that requires ratification, from the negotiations to its domestic application. Which organs are involved, and which treaties need parliamentary approval? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Federal President issues full powers and ratifies (Art 65 B-VG); political and law-amending or law-supplementing treaties first need approval of the Nationalrat (Art 50 B-VG) with Bundesrat participation; the instrument is deposited or exchanged and the treaty is published in the BGBl III.
• Negotiations and signature: by representatives with full powers from the Federal President (Art 65(1) B-VG: he represents the Republic externally and concludes treaties).
• Council of Ministers decides to submit the treaty to Parliament (government bill with explanatory notes).
• Nationalrat approval (Art 50(1) B-VG) for (1) political treaties and treaties amending or supplementing laws, and (2) treaties amending the EU founding treaties (qualified majorities in both chambers).
• Bundesrat: participates like in legislation; its consent is required where the treaty regulates matters within the autonomous competence of the Länder (Art 50(2) B-VG).
• Possible Erfüllungsvorbehalt (Art 50(2) B-VG): implementation by laws; no direct applicability until then.
• Ratification: instrument signed by the Federal President, countersigned by the Federal Chancellor (and ministers) (Art 67 B-VG), sealed; deposit with the depositary or exchange with the partner State.
• International entry into force per the treaty (Art 24 VCLT); publication by the Federal Chancellor in BGBl III (Art 49 B-VG) → domestic applicability.
• Other treaties (neither political nor law-amending): concluded without Parliament — by the Federal President or, on his authorization, by the Federal Government or ministers (Art 66(2) B-VG). Länder may conclude treaties with neighbouring States in their own sphere (Art 16 B-VG).
Memorise: Full powers (BP, Art 65) → sign → Council of Ministers → Nationalrat (Art 50) + Bundesrat (Länder) → [Erfüllungsvorbehalt] → ratification (BP + countersignature, Art 67) → deposit → BGBl III (Art 49).

cards.q: How do customary international law and treaties become part of Austrian law? Explain the Erfüllungsvorbehalt and whether an individual can rely on such a treaty before Austrian courts. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Custom applies automatically as federal law under Art 9(1) B-VG; treaties become part of domestic law through approval and publication — but where the Nationalrat attaches an Erfüllungsvorbehalt, courts and authorities may apply the treaty only through implementing statutes.
• Art 9(1) B-VG: the generally recognized rules of international law are valid parts of federal law — automatic, general incorporation of custom (e.g. state immunity, state succession), no act of transformation.
• Treaties: after approval under Art 50 B-VG and publication in BGBl III (Art 49 B-VG) part of the domestic order, generally at the rank of statutes (exception: e.g. the ECHR has constitutional rank since 1964).
• Direct application also presupposes a self-executing provision — precise enough for courts to apply without further legislation (contrast Art 86 Rome Statute, a duty addressed to the State).
• Erfüllungsvorbehalt (Art 50(2) B-VG): the Nationalrat resolves that the treaty 'is to be fulfilled by the enactment of laws' (e.g. the Racial Discrimination Convention, 1972) → individuals cannot invoke it directly; only the implementing laws apply.
• Internationally Austria is bound from entry into force regardless (Art 26, 27 VCLT); failure to pass the implementing laws is a breach.
Memorise: Custom → Art 9(1) B-VG automatic · treaty → Art 50 approval + BGBl III · Erfüllungsvorbehalt = no direct application, international obligation unaffected.
